tags.gist: Praises the paper's candor, supports its general architecture, and aims criticism at places that would not survive a real submission or failure.
Wants the two axes reconciled with ISO 14971 and the omitted probability of an error escaping detection added.
Wants an explicit published table linking each risk tier to the least evidence required; without it the approach is case-by-case review renamed.
Would allow synthetic data for finding failures and rare events but never to establish performance rates, since it supplies no valid denominator.
Rejects the median clinician standard in favor of prespecified acceptance criteria from decision consequences, with panels as validated adjudication instruments.
Wants independence required for any supervisory agent used as evidence, since a same-model monitor shares the device's failure modes.
Wants inability to pin a version-identified third-party model with change notice treated as a design deficiency, calling this the paper's largest gap.
Wants PCCPs for generative systems built on invariants, locked instruments, thresholds and protocols, rather than on lists of planned changes.
Calls the two axes necessary but insufficient because they ignore how likely an incorrect output is to be acted on.
Argues the grid captures severity but not probability as ISO 14971 does, and fluent generative errors are inherently harder to detect.
Wants detectability added as an explicit dimension, with reversibility, safeguards, time pressure and traceability as its determinants.
Wants FDA to state how the grid relates to a manufacturer's ISO 14971 risk file, to avoid a duplicate FDA-specific taxonomy.
Objects that directiveness is an emergent output property, so sponsors cannot honestly attest to it at design time.
Wants sponsors to specify a directiveness ceiling, its controls and a measured escape rate, with classification resting on the ceiling and bound.
Wants risk to turn on the user's realistic verification path at the moment of reliance rather than on patient versus clinician category.
Wants risk assessed against foreseeable off-label users, crediting technical enforcement of user scope but not labeling alone.
Wants the session, not the turn, declared the unit of intended use and evaluation, with adversarial multi-turn testing of escape rates.
Wants FDA to say plainly that turn-level evaluation of a conversational device is insufficient on its own.
Wants the escalation trade-off prespecified as an asymmetric acceptance criterion with clinical justification, not characterized after the fact.
Says over-escalation harms are diffuse, delayed and seldom traced back to the device, so postmarket mechanisms under-detect them.
Broadly accepts the competency approach but says the clinician analogy rests on an unstated assumption doing more work than it can bear.
Argues credentialing can be evidentiarily light only because of continuous individual accountability that a deployed model lacks.
Notes generative failures are not legible the way human errors are and can hide from aggregate performance measurement.
Wants the competency framing kept as structure while FDA states the analogy justifies the shape of evidence, not its quantity.
Wants a published, stable table giving minimum benchmarking, confirmation tier, third-party role and monitoring for each risk band, with a deviation pathway.
Wants adversarial input such as prompt injection and jailbreaks as a distinct benchmarking element tied to cybersecurity expectations.
Wants citation fidelity measured separately, since a fabricated plausible reference turns the user's verification safeguard into a hazard.
Wants boundary behavior tested, distinguishing graceful degradation with visible uncertainty from sharp failure while confidence stays high.
Declines to name external standards and asks FDA to survey which AI evaluation standards are mature enough to recognize.
Says public benchmark results on third-party models are uninterpretable without a dated training cutoff attestation, preferring temporally held-out data.
Wants sponsors to document, per benchmark, the real-world behavior it predicts and the limits of that link, as analytical validation.
Would permit sponsor benchmarks if locked before evaluation, attested unused in development, and partly escrowed with FDA or a third party.
Wants public benchmarks treated as necessary screens that are never counted as proof of effectiveness.
Raises a periodically refreshed, never-published evaluation set held by FDA or a recognized steward as a direction worth evaluating.
Supports the ladder but wants the rung set by the published risk mapping rather than by sponsor justification.
Wants shadow deployment presumed for intermediate risk, since curated retrospective inputs omit the malformed cases that cause real-world failure.
Wants the anticipated input distribution characterized prospectively and confirmation evidence labeled with its population and setting.
Because outputs vary at fixed input, wants performance characterized over repeated runs with within-input and between-input variance reported separately.
Wants acceptance criteria judged on a lower confidence bound rather than a point estimate.
Wants temperature and similar sampling settings treated as specified device parameters under change control.
Recommends against pooling benchmark and confirmation evidence, with confirmation governing acceptance and benchmarking as support and baseline.
Agrees with the framing and stresses correlated failure: a same-family generator reproduces the device's blind spots and manufactures false confidence.
Wants a line drawn by purpose: synthetic data for stress testing and rare scenarios, never for performance rates needing a real denominator.
Wants same-family synthetic generation prohibited for subgroup performance claims, the place correlated blind spots hurt most.
Wants any synthetic generator's identity, provenance and lineage disclosed, with its relation to the device's model stated.
Knows no validated method for showing a synthetic population matches a real one, and asks FDA to proceed as if none exists.
Rejects the median clinician as primary standard: it is unmeasured, a moving target, and anchors the bar to practice variation not patient benefit.
Wants prespecified, defended clinical acceptance criteria derived from what happens when the device is wrong.
Wants clinician panels treated as measurement instruments with prespecified composition, protocol, blinding and reported inter-rater reliability.
Wants the comparator to match the labeled intended user, since benchmarking a primary care tool against subspecialists measures the wrong thing.
Where labeling requires human review, wants team performance primary and designed to detect automation bias with confidently wrong cases.
Supports comparing against care in the device's absence, since access-expanding devices often replace no or delayed assessment.
Wants the counterfactual empirically characterized per setting and carried into labeling so a low-bar authorization cannot creep in scope.
Finds third parties well suited to benchmark administration, escrow of held-out sets and clinical adjudication.
Wants published recognition criteria so qualifying bodies are not chosen at discretion and entry is contestable.
Wants a body that advised a sponsor disqualified from assessing that device, as a rule rather than a disclosure.
Wants public disclosure of financial ties and revenue concentration between assessing bodies and sponsors.
Wants third-party assessment kept optional, never a mandatory gate, to avoid chokepoints that burden small developers.
Notes third-party capacity for generative devices does not yet exist at scale and asks the paper to acknowledge the build-out timeline.
Urges caution for multimodal and world models, whose thin benchmarks mean confirmation evidence has to bear correspondingly more of the weight.
Finds the trade appealing but asks FDA to publish data on postmarket obligation completion for software devices before relying on it.
Wants monitoring made a binding condition of authorization with prespecified triggers and automatic consequences, including suspension of marketing.
Wants sponsors to demonstrate a data path linking outputs to observable clinical consequences before monitoring can justify less premarket evidence.
Says the trade is unavailable where harm would build up more quickly than the monitoring cadence can catch degradation.
Says irreversible harm forecloses the trade, because postmarket detection would only audit damage already done.
Wants FDA to state that reduced premarket evidence is unavailable in the high-consequence, high-activity region of the grid.
Finds the three approaches complementary but wants cadence event-driven with a calendar floor rather than calendar-driven.
Lists triggers such as model, prompt, corpus or sampling changes, input shift and complaint thresholds, with an annual or tighter floor.
Wants reassessment triggers defined as change-control triggers inside the QMS rather than as a separate process.
Accepts automated supervision as unavoidable but warns a same-model supervisor shares the device's blind spots and confirms nothing.
Wants supervisors built on a different model family and provider, or failure-mode correlation reported with credit scaled to independence.
Wants the supervisor validated as an instrument by sensitivity for serious harms against human adjudication, re-measured over time.
Would limit the supervisor to triaging outputs for human review, keeping the adjudicated endpoint human.
Wants any modification of the supervisory agent to prompt the same reassessment a device change would.
Wants FDA to state that signal may come from anywhere but the duty to investigate and report stays with the manufacturer.
Flags unresolved MDR reportability of caught hallucinations and suggests an aggregate rate-based channel for near-misses.
Supports a locked baseline and would categorize changes by whether the locked evaluation instrument stays valid, not by change size.
Proposes three tiers: no re-benchmarking for output-neutral changes, QMS-managed full re-benchmarking, and premarket submission for model-family or scope changes.
Insists the benchmark suite cannot be modified within the QMS tier; changing the instrument is always a submission event.
Would invert the PCCP so it prespecifies the invariants that hold after every change, since future modifications cannot be enumerated.
Lists the invariants: escrowed suite, thresholds with subgroup margins, verification protocol, rollback criteria, scoped categories and notification duties.
Says escrowing the suite and sending every change to it through a submission are the proposal itself, not optional features.
Describes hosted endpoints updated without notice and short deprecation timelines as a condition no quality system can accommodate.
Wants FDA to state that execution against a pinned, version-identified endpoint is expected and inability to pin is a design deficiency.
Wants contractual change notice long enough to complete re-benchmarking, plus a guaranteed minimum period before pinned versions are deprecated.
Wants continuous canary probes against the live endpoint as an expected monitoring element to detect silent upstream change.
Wants provider-forced migration treated as a full submission-level change, with a validated fallback planned in advance.
Says a master file would be most valuable as a current record of a model's versioning, deprecation and change-notification practices.
Agrees developers have little reason to catalog their own flaws for an agency that regulates a different company's product.
Wants the program created with a default that, absent a master file, the device maker bears the full model characterization burden, creating procurement pull.
Suggests contents including version lineage, training cutoff date, deprecation policy, failure modes and evaluations, with a currency requirement.
Cautions that a master file is context for evaluating the configured device and never a partial substitute for it.
Wants acceptance criteria stated for the completed task, since per-step accuracy compounds into much lower end-to-end reliability.
Wants a locked inventory of every action classified by reversibility, with irreversible actions confirmed by a qualified user.
Wants least-privilege tool access per deployment, cross-referenced to existing cybersecurity expectations.
Wants audit logs that can rebuild the whole trajectory reviewed as an explicit premarket element for agentic devices.
Wants agentic devices presumptively excluded from the reduced-premarket-evidence pathway, since their errors propagate fastest.
Repeats that publishing the risk-tier-to-evidence mapping is what makes a risk-based framework least burdensome.
Wants the framework to draw on existing ISO 14971 files, design controls and change control rather than parallel artifacts.
Asks FDA to settle whether and how generative outputs are reportable under MDR, since every postmarket element depends on it.
Repeats that expecting model version pinning as a design control is achievable now and closes the largest gap.
Asks FDA to identify which proposals, such as enforceable postmarket conditions or developer obligations, would need new legal authority.
Wants FDA to state the framework can conclude an intended use is not supportable, so it is an evaluation framework, not an entry pathway.
Appreciates FDA publishing preliminary thinking and calls the competency framing a real contribution.
Worries flexibility outruns the needed infrastructure of trusted benchmarks, settled reporting rules and controllable dependencies, which should come first.
